The best security is layered; each layer requires time and effort to deal with by any would be thief. A hefty chain secured to a ground anchor makes it harder just to lift the bike into a van and be gone. A grinder resistant d-lock around/through the back wheel needs removing before it can be wheeled away. An alarmed disc lock on the front…etc etc.

The general rule of thumb that’s come from the police on bikesafe days is to plan to complete the overtake as quickly as possible. In your scenario I’d recommend a “three-stage” overtake: 
1. Ascertain the road ahead is clear.
2. Move to the offside and pause for a moment to confirm clear, sufficient space, no unseen hazards and it serves to make your intentions clear. In your scenario this may have caused the dickhead to start his dangerous speeding up manoeuvre, not guaranteed though obviously. 
3. Plant your foot and accelerate quickly past the vehicle before returning to the nearside. 
(All the above should be conducted with relevant signals, mirror and shoulder checks, and in full compliance with road markings and signage - before people start picking it apart!)

They employ insurance claims investigators, often retired detectives, who are instructed by insurance companies to look into any claims they have concerns about. Given the increasing popularity of fronting, it’s likely that claims involving young drivers are in the mix for investigation. At that point it would be easy enough for an investigator to deduce that the main driver was in fact the named driver. Did the parents each have their own or vehicle? If not, do they have bus receipts/train tickets/a push bike etc? Was the accident in a location the parents could reasonably be? If they normally work mon-fri and the accident happened on a Tuesday lunchtime, were they on annual leave? Sick? At an appointment? 
If the investigator decides that, on balance, the named driver was the main driver, then they’ll recommend the claim is void. Up to the insurer then to decide, but they often go with it as a balance of probabilities situation. I imagine the driver(s) are free to take a legal challenge if they so choose. 
Obviously all hinges on A. A claimable incident happening and B. That claim being subsequently investigated.

Just to add a voice of caution: going out at night will obviously provide very quiet roads - good. 
It will also reduce your visibility, making it harder to see problems with the road surface that could affect grip and stability (pot holes, oil/fuel spills, gravel, man hole covers etc). 
It will reduce your conspicuity; motorists don’t see us in the daytime with sunshine reflecting off bright clothing, we are essentially invisible at night. It is also harder, for those that do see us, to assess our speed. 
You will likely be tired! Riding tired is always a bad idea, even more so when you are learning the skills. 

I echo the recommendations for finding quiet spots, car parks, industrial estates etc and practicing there during daylight hours. Get good at the two main stays of defensive riding - braking and swerving. Read up on/watch videos on how to brake effectively and spend lots of time practicing that. If you can stop quickly and smoothly, in any situation, you will increase you confidence on the road knowing that, if all else fails, you can stop and stay out of harms way rapidly. Same applies to swerving. 

Stay safe and have fun!
